whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the B2C Commerce Developer exam for?

personas.label: SFCC developers
personas.description: You build and customize B2C Commerce storefronts using SFRA, ISML, and server-side JavaScript and want the certification to validate your full-stack SFCC skills.

personas.label: Full-stack commerce engineers
personas.description: You work with controllers, templates, OCAPI/SCAPI, and Business Manager configuration and need a credential that covers the entire SFCC development stack.

personas.label: Technical leads
personas.description: You manage cartridge architecture, deployment pipelines, and storefront performance for B2C Commerce projects and want to formalize your technical leadership.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the B2C Commerce Developer Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The B2C Commerce Developer exam is considered one of the harder Salesforce developer certifications. The ~65% passing score is moderate, but the exam covers the full SFCC stack, from SFRA architecture and ISML templates to OCAPI/SCAPI integration and Business Manager configuration, demanding broad and deep hands-on experience.
bullets: ~65% passing score: moderate on paper, but the breadth of topics (SFRA, scripting, APIs, data model, deployment) makes it demanding.
Full-stack depth: questions span server-side controllers, ISML templates, client-side JavaScript, and Business Manager operations, so you cannot skip any layer.
Hands-on SFRA experience essential: real project experience with SFRA controller development and at least one OCAPI or SCAPI integration is the strongest preparation.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Spend time in a B2C Commerce sandbox building custom controllers, overriding SFRA templates, and configuring jobs in Business Manager before booking the exam.

examFormat.heading: B2C Commerce Developer Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in-person. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Around 40-50% of questions are scenario-based. Common patterns describe a storefront customization requirement and ask which SFRA pattern, controller method, or API approach meets it. Expect questions on cartridge path resolution, template overrides, and OCAPI resource configuration.
bestWayToPass: Master the cartridge override pattern: Know how the cartridge path resolves controllers and templates, and when to use server.extend vs. server.replace.
Build with SFRA hands-on: Create custom controllers, override ISML templates, and work with the dw.* API in a sandbox environment.
Study OCAPI and SCAPI: Understand the Shop API vs. Data API, how authentication works for headless scenarios, and when to use each API.
Know Business Manager inside out: Practice configuring site preferences, running jobs, managing code versions, and diagnosing issues using the request log and pipeline profiler.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers full-stack SFCC development: SFRA cartridge architecture, ISML templates, controller scripting, OCAPI/SCAPI integration, and Business Manager configuration.

keyConcepts.h2: B2C Commerce Developer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: SFRA Architecture: Cartridges & Override Pattern
blocks.body: **SFRA** is the Salesforce B2C Commerce reference architecture built on a cartridge system. **cartridges** are modular packages containing controllers, templates, models, and static assets. The cartridge path (configured in **Business Manager**) defines override priority, the leftmost cartridge wins. To customize, create a custom cartridge that overrides specific controllers or templates without editing base cartridges. This keeps base cartridge upgrades non-destructive. The `server.extend` and `server.replace` patterns in controllers allow adding before/after steps or completely replacing a route. The developer exam tests the correct use of the override pattern and common mistakes that break cartridge path resolution.

blocks.heading: Controllers, Scripts & Server-Side Logic
blocks.body: **SFRA** controllers are JavaScript modules using the `server` framework. Routes handle GET and POST requests and render templates or return JSON. Middleware functions (authentication, CSRF, consent) can be prepended to any route. Models and helpers contain business logic separated from controllers. `dw.system`, `dw.order`, `dw.catalog`, the Digital SDK, provides access to Commerce Cloud server-side APIs. Custom scripts (`.js` files in `cartridge/scripts/`) encapsulate reusable logic. The exam tests how to add a middleware step to an existing controller route, how to call a custom script from a controller, and common governor limit considerations in server-side scripts.

blocks.heading: Templates (ISML) & Client-Side Assets
blocks.body: ISML (Internet Store Markup Language) is the server-side templating language. `<isinclude>` embeds sub-templates. `<isloop>` iterates collections. `<isset>` assigns variables. `<isif>` handles conditionals. Resource bundles (properties files) provide localized strings. Static assets (JS, CSS, images) are organized in `cartridge/static/` and referenced via `URLUtils.staticURL()`. Webpack compiles and bundles client-side JS in **SFRA**. SASS is compiled to CSS. Client-side JavaScript uses jQuery and Bootstrap in SFRA. The exam tests ISML syntax, how to pass data from controller to template via `pdict`, and how to add a new client-side component.

blocks.heading: Jobs, Feeds & Business Manager Configuration
blocks.body: Commerce Cloud Jobs run server-side scripts on a schedule or on-demand. Jobs process product feeds (import/export), order exports, and inventory updates. The Job Framework uses steps configured in **Business Manager**. IMPEX (Import/Export) handles large data loads via XML or CSV files placed in the IMPEX directory. Site Preferences store admin-configurable settings accessible in code via `dw.system.Site.current.preferences`. Custom Attributes extend standard objects (products, orders, customers) in Business Manager. The exam tests Job configuration, IMPEX file formats, and how to read custom site preferences in controller logic.

blocks.heading: Testing, Debugging & Deployment
blocks.body: Commerce Cloud development uses the `sgmf-scripts` (**SFRA** build tools) and Salesforce Commerce Cloud CLI (`sfcc-ci`) for deployment. Code deployment uploads **cartridges** to a code version, which is then activated. The Request Log and Custom Log APIs (`dw.system.Logger`) support debugging. The Pipeline Profiler identifies slow controller routes. Functional tests use `mochawesome` reports. Unit testing is done with jest and `dw-api-types` mocks for Digital SDK. The exam tests the deployment sequence (cartridge upload → code version activation), how to write a testable controller with mocked dependencies, and how to diagnose errors using **Business Manager** logs.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce B2C Commerce Developer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The B2C Commerce Developer exam tests hands-on SFCC development: ISML templates, controller development (SFRA), and script development. Focus on the SFRA architecture and how to implement common storefront customizations.

blocks.heading: SFRA Architecture
blocks.body: Know the **storefront** Reference Architecture (**SFRA**) MVC pattern: Routes (controllers), Models (data layer), Templates (ISML views), and how **cartridges** layer on top of SFRA using the cartridge path.

blocks.heading: Controller Development
blocks.body: Know how to create custom routes (server.get/post/append/prepend/replace), use middleware for authentication/CSRF protection, and how to return JSON responses or render ISML templates from controllers.

blocks.heading: ISML Templates
blocks.body: Know ISML syntax: <isset>, <isif>, <isloop>, <isinclude>, <isreplace>, and how to use locale, currency, and content asset tags. Understand how template caching affects dynamic content rendering.

blocks.heading: Script Development
blocks.body: Know how to write CommonJS-style scripts in SFCC, use the dw.* API (dw.catalog, dw.order, dw.customer), and how to call web services from scripts using the dw.net.HTTPClient.

blocks.heading: Business Manager Configuration
blocks.body: Know key **Business Manager** configurations: catalog setup, pricebook management, promotion configuration, **storefront** configuration (site preferences), and how to use the UX Studio for cartridge management.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After Developer
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this certification, common next steps in the developer track:

sampleQuestions.question: A developer needs to add a field to the product object that the storefront will display. Where is this defined?
options: In the system object metadata as a custom attribute
In a new custom object created alongside the standard product object
In the site preference settings for the storefront being developed
In a cartridge template that renders the value directly from the catalogue
sampleQuestions.explanation: Custom attributes extend the standard system objects, which is how product data beyond the built-in fields is held.
whyWrong: A parallel custom object breaks the relationship to the product.
Site preferences hold configuration, not product attributes.
A template renders data; it does not define where the data lives.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the cartridge path?
options: It defines which payment providers are enabled for the storefront
It controls the order in which jobs execute on the instance overnight
It decides which cartridge's version of a file wins
It lists the catalogues that have been assigned to the current site
sampleQuestions.explanation: The cartridge path is searched in order, so a file in an earlier cartridge overrides the same path in a later one. That is the basis of customisation without editing base code.
whyWrong: Payment configuration is held in site preferences.
Job order is configured in the job framework.
Catalogue assignment is separate site configuration.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer must customise checkout without modifying the base cartridge. What is the correct approach?
options: Override the relevant files in a custom cartridge
Copy the whole base cartridge and rename it as the project's own version
Disable the base cartridge entirely and rebuild checkout from scratch
Edit the base cartridge directly and keep a record of every change made
sampleQuestions.explanation: Putting your own version earlier on the cartridge path lets you change behaviour while leaving the base code upgradeable.
whyWrong: Wholesale copying inherits the maintenance burden of the entire cartridge.
Rebuilding checkout discards tested, compliant functionality.
Editing base code makes every future platform upgrade painful.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a controller do in a B2C Commerce storefront?
options: It stores the product data that the storefront pages will display
It handles a request and decides what to render
It schedules the import jobs that refresh the catalogue each night
It defines the visual styling applied across the storefront's pages
sampleQuestions.explanation: Controllers receive the request. Run the server-side logic and choose the template or JSON response to return.
whyWrong: Product data lives in the catalogue and system objects.
Imports are configured as jobs.
Styling is handled by stylesheets and templates.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer needs to share logic between two controllers. What is the appropriate structure?
options: A script module that both controllers require
A template fragment that each of the controllers renders in turn
A copy of the same function placed in each of the two controllers
A custom object holding the logic as a stored configuration value
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shared server-side logic belongs in a module, so there is one implementation for both callers to use.
whyWrong: Templates render output; they are not a place for business logic.
Duplicated functions drift apart and double the bug surface.
Custom objects store data rather than executable logic.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does a developer need to be careful with API quotas on the platform?
options: Quotas set the maximum number of products a catalogue may contain
Quotas control how often the storefront's cache can be invalidated
Exceeding them degrades or fails the request
Quotas determine how many cartridges a site is permitted to use
sampleQuestions.explanation: The platform enforces limits on operations such as object queries per request, and breaching them causes warnings and eventually failures.
whyWrong: Catalogue size is a data concern rather than a quota.
Cache invalidation is configured separately.
Cartridge count is not governed by API quotas.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the role of OCAPI or SCAPI in a B2C Commerce implementation?
options: Importing the product catalogue from the client's own backend system
Rendering the storefront pages that shoppers see in their browser
Defining the business manager screens used by the client's merchants
Exposing commerce data and operations to external clients
sampleQuestions.explanation: These APIs let external applications, including headless front ends and integrations, read and write commerce data.
whyWrong: Catalogue import is handled by the job framework and feeds.
Storefront rendering is done by controllers and templates.
Business Manager screens are platform functionality.

sampleQuestions.question: A price must differ for members of a loyalty scheme. What mechanism supports this?
options: A separate catalogue containing a duplicate of every eligible product
A customer group with its own price book
A promotion applied by the shopper entering a code at the checkout
A custom attribute on the product holding the member price value
sampleQuestions.explanation: Customer groups let the platform resolve a different price book for a defined set of shoppers.
whyWrong: Duplicating the catalogue is unmaintainable.
A code requires shopper action and is not automatic membership pricing.
An attribute holds a number but does not make the platform charge it.

sampleQuestions.question: What should a developer consider when writing a job that processes the full catalogue?
options: Disabling the storefront while the job is running to avoid conflicts
Chunking the work so it stays within limits
Processing the records one at a time to guarantee nothing is skipped
Running the job during peak trading so errors are noticed quickly
sampleQuestions.explanation: Large jobs need to process in chunks with checkpoints, or they exhaust resources and fail partway through.
whyWrong: Taking the storefront down for a routine job is not acceptable.
Row-by-row processing is what fails at catalogue scale.
Peak trading is the worst time to run heavy batch work.

sampleQuestions.question: Why is content caching important on a storefront?
options: It ensures the catalogue data is always completely up to date
It keeps response times low under real traffic
It removes the need to consider API quotas within controllers
It guarantees that every shopper sees personalised pricing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Caching is what allows a storefront to serve high traffic, and getting cache boundaries right is a core performance concern.
whyWrong: Caching trades freshness for speed, so it does the opposite of this.
Quotas still apply to uncached work.
Aggressive caching makes personalisation harder, not guaranteed.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer finds personalised content being served from cache to the wrong shoppers. What is the cause?
options: An API quota being exceeded during the rendering of the page
A missing custom attribute on the product records being displayed
Personalised output cached without varying on the shopper
The cartridge path placing the custom cartridge in the wrong position
sampleQuestions.explanation: Caching a response that depends on who is viewing it, without including that in the cache key, serves one shopper's content to another.
whyWrong: Quota breaches cause failures rather than cross-contamination.
A missing attribute would show empty data rather than someone else's.
Cartridge order affects which code runs, not cache correctness.

sampleQuestions.question: What distinguishes a storefront catalogue from a master catalogue?
options: One is editable by merchants and the other only by developers
One holds physical goods while the other holds digital products only
One applies to a single site and the other to a single locale
One organises products for browsing; the other owns them
sampleQuestions.explanation: Products are defined in a master catalogue and then assigned into a storefront catalogue's category structure for navigation.
whyWrong: Both are managed through Business Manager.
Both can hold any product type.
Locale is handled separately from catalogue structure.

sampleQuestions.question: A client wants a headless front end calling the commerce platform. What changes for the developer?
options: Jobs must be rewritten because they cannot run without a storefront
The cartridge path is no longer used for any purpose at all
Custom attributes can no longer be added to the system objects
Rendering moves out and the platform serves data
sampleQuestions.explanation: In a headless setup the front end owns presentation and the platform is consumed through its APIs, so server-side templating largely falls away.
whyWrong: Jobs run independently of how the front end is built.
Cartridges remain relevant for server-side logic and hooks.
Object extension works as before.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the safest way to handle a shopper's payment details in a custom checkout?
options: Let the payment provider capture them directly
Pass them through the controller and log them for later reconciliation
Store them in a custom attribute on the shopper's own profile record
Hold them in session until the order has been successfully placed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Card data should never touch your application. The provider's hosted fields or redirect keeps it out of scope and out of your logs.
whyWrong: Logging payment details is exactly what must never happen.
Storing card details on a profile is a serious compliance breach.
Holding card data in session still brings it into scope.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes what a developer is responsible for on a B2C Commerce project?
options: The visual design of the storefront's pages and brand styling
The merchandising decisions about which products to promote
Storefront behaviour, integrations and data extensions
The hosting infrastructure the commerce platform itself runs on
sampleQuestions.explanation: The developer builds and customises how the storefront behaves, extends the data model and connects the platform to other systems.
whyWrong: Visual design is usually produced by designers.
Merchandising is a business user's role in Business Manager.
Infrastructure is operated by Salesforce.
